transcript.text: hi, we keep losing customers every month and i dont know what to do about it

Losing customers month after month is a common problem, and it is usually fixable once you can see *who* is leaving, *when*, and *what they had in common*. I can help on any of those fronts.

Most of these need a table of your customers — even a rough export from your CRM or billing system is enough to start. If you're not sure what you have, the first option below is the gentlest way in.

Here's where we could go:

Good choice — this is the one that pays off fastest, because a list of at-risk customers lets you act *before* they're gone.

I've started the churn model. Here's how it works, in short: the model looks at your customers who *already* left, finds what their records had in common, then scores everyone still with you on how closely they match that pattern.

To get going, I need your customer data — an export from your CRM, billing system or a spreadsheet is fine. Two tables is even better. Most useful, roughly in order:

- **Who left, and when** — a status column (active / cancelled) or a table of cancellation dates. This is what the model learns from.
- **Who is still here** — one row per current customer, with the same detail columns.
- **Their detail** — how long they've been with you, what plan and price they're on, how much they use the product (logins, orders, calls, hours — whatever yours tracks), support tickets, payment failures, contract terms.

The richer the usage and billing columns, the sharper the list. Demographics alone rarely predict much.

Two things to tell me along with the file:

1. **What "lost" means for you** — cancelled subscription, no purchase in X months, contract not renewed? I need one clear rule.
2. **How far ahead you want to see** — next month, next 3 months, next 6? A shorter window is easier to get right and more useful for saving them.

If your data is spread across several files or you're not sure what you can pull, send what you've got and I'll work out what's usable before anything else happens.

choices.title: See how big the leak actually is
choices.what: Turn your customer history into plain numbers: how many you lose each month, churn rate over time, and which customer groups are leaving fastest. You get: A clear picture of where the losses are concentrated, so you know what to fix first. Trade-off: It tells you what is happening and to whom, but it won't predict who leaves next month. Effort: Light — needs a customer table with dates or a current/churned flag.

choices.title: Flag the customers likely to leave next
choices.what: Build a model that scores every current customer on their chance of churning in the coming period, based on past leavers. You get: A ranked list of at-risk customers you can act on now, before they go. Trade-off: Needs enough past churn examples to learn from, and some clean-up of the data first. Effort: Medium — a proper modelling job.

choices.title: Work out why they leave and what to do
choices.what: A written brief that pulls together the likely causes of your churn and lays out the practical options, with tradeoffs, for reducing it. You get: A decision-ready answer rather than a pile of numbers. Trade-off: Best with some supporting data; without it the reasoning leans on general patterns rather than your own customers. Effort: Light to medium.

choices.title: Get your data in order first
choices.what: Clean up and merge the files you already have — customers, usage, billing, support tickets — into one workable table. You get: A single tidy table ready for measurement, modelling or reporting down the line. Trade-off: Prep work only; no answers out of it on its own. Effort: Light — depends on how messy the files are.

transcript.text:
That one's already underway — good.

Now it's waiting on your data. Whenever you're ready, send the export (spreadsheet or CSV is fine; one file or several, whatever you have) and tell me two things:

- **Your rule for "lost"** — cancelled outright, or no activity for X months?
- **How far ahead to look** — next month, next 3, next 6?

The moment the file lands, I'll check what's actually in it before modelling: whether it holds a clear record of who left and when, how many past leavers there are to learn from, and which columns would unfairly tip off the model (for instance a "days since last login" field that only gets filled in after someone cancels — those get set aside). Then you'll get a ranked list of at-risk customers, plus the handful of traits that separate stayers from leavers, so you know what to *do* with the list rather than just having it.

If pulling the export is the awkward part, tell me what system your customer records live in and I'll talk you through the simplest version that would work.
ok. it’s an excel from billing with cust no, start date, plan, monthly bill, support calls, and left yes/no. i don’t have the exact date they left, only if left. we need top 300 next month.

That's a workable file. Missing the exact date isn't a blocker — here's what changes because of it, so nothing surprises you later.

**What the model will do.** With "left yes/no" plus the other columns, it learns what your leavers look like compared with your stayers — plan, bill size, support calls, how long they'd been with you — then ranks everyone still on the books by how closely they match the leaver profile. That part needs no dates.

**What "next month" then means.** The score tells you *who looks like they're going*, not *when*. So a top 300 straight off that score risks filling up with people who have a year of patience left. To keep the list useful I'll order it by churn score **and** how recently the signs showed up, so the 300 are the ones looking most like leavers right now, not just ever. Worth knowing up front: we'll get you 300 actionable names, but the honest claim is "these 300 are the likeliest to go," not "these 300 will go by the 31st."

**The one column that would sharpen this a lot.** A billing export nearly always has a last invoice month or last payment date somewhere, even when there's no cancellation date. If you can spot that and keep it in, we get real timing on the shortlist instead of inferred timing. Tenure from start date we can already calculate, so don't go hunting for that.

**One caution.** How are support calls counted — total lifetime, or over the last 30 or 90 days? It matters, because a "cancel my account" phone call recorded after someone has left is a giveaway the model shouldn't see, and it would quietly flatter the results. If your calls column is lifetime-to-date, I'll treat it carefully rather than at face value.

Three quick numbers so I can set this up sensibly, then send the file and I'll get going:

1. Roughly how many customers are in the sheet in total? Top 300 means a very different thing if you have 2,000 accounts versus 50,000.
2. Roughly how many are marked "left"? Under a few dozen and the pattern gets thin.
3. Support calls — lifetime, or recent window?

And one thing to decide on your side, not mine: 300 people who look like they're about to leave is only valuable if you can reach them this month. If that's too many for whoever handles retention, say so and I'll rank them properly but tell you where the useful cut-off actually sits.
about 9k in file. i think a few hundred marked left, we lose about 3% a month. support calls not sure if lifetime or recent. 300 is all we can call. sending file.

Those numbers line up well, and one of them is worth putting in front of you: 3% of 9,000 is about 270 customers a month. Your calling capacity is 300. So the list you're asking for is almost exactly the size of the monthly leak — which means if the ranking is any good, you're not picking a lucky few, you're reaching nearly everyone who's about to go. That's the best setup for actually moving the churn number.

Two honest notes on what you've told me.

**A few hundred leavers is enough, but it means keeping things plain.** The model learns only from the rows marked "left." A few hundred is workable, so I'll keep the model simple and check its score against rows it hasn't seen, rather than dress up a big confident number from a small sample. Expect a shortlist with real signal in it, and a straight answer about how much.

**The 270-versus-few-hundred gap is worth a second look.** You lose roughly 270 a month, yet only a few hundred in the whole file are flagged as gone. That usually means one of two things: the billing export only keeps a short history, or the left flag only covers recent departures. Either is fine, but it tells us something about what the model can see — if it only knows about people who left in the last month or two, it's learning the last-stage signs of churn, which actually suits a 30-day list rather than working against it.

Once the file lands I'll settle the support calls question myself rather than making you check — a quick comparison of call counts between stayers and leavers will show whether it's a lifetime total or a recent window, and whether any of those calls are happening *after* someone has already left, which is the one way this data could quietly cheat.

I'll also look at whether the leaver rows have their bill and plan fields blank or zeroed. Billing exports sometimes switch a cancelled account's monthly bill to 0, and if the model gets to see that, it scores perfectly and means nothing — every current customer has a non-zero bill, so none of them could ever look like a leaver.

Send it over and I'll take it from there.
